title: Six days of making (Genesis 1:6–31)
hook: sky, sea, land, lights, creatures, each day closing "and it was good"

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bereshit. In the beginning, a voice, and light answered. Your line was words make worlds. Did your kind sentence get said? Day twenty-three.

An empty apartment fills up in a certain order. First the rooms: walls, a floor, a window that lets the light in. Only then do you bring in what fills them: a lamp for the corner, fish in a tank, a cat on the windowsill, people around a table. Nobody hangs a picture before there's a wall. Back on day six you met the refrain of the first chapter, and it was good. Today we walk through the days themselves, sky, sea, land, lights and creatures, and notice that the chapter is built a lot like that apartment.
screen: `AN EMPTY APARTMENT.` → `FIRST THE ROOMS.` → `THEN WHAT FILLS THEM.`

segments.voice: Here are the six days. One: light, separated from dark. Two: a dome of sky, separating the waters above from the waters below. Three: dry land appears, and plants grow on it. Four: the sun, the moon and the stars. Five: fish in the sea and birds in the sky. Six: animals on the land, and then human beings. Some readers notice a pattern. The first three days make spaces: day, sky and sea, land. The next three fill them, in the same order: lights for the day, fish and birds for the sea and sky, creatures for the land. Rooms, then furniture. Now a puzzle the rabbis loved. There's light on day one, but no sun until day four. So what was that first light? The Talmud says it was a special light, by which a person could see from one end of the world to the other, and God hid it away for the righteous in the time to come. Some readers notice something else: the text never names the sun and moon. It calls them the greater light and the lesser light, lamps set in the sky to do a job. And the word for day, yom? Jewish readers have disagreed about whether these are days of twenty-four hours, and the chapter doesn't stop to say. What it does say, over and over, is that each thing is made "after its kind," each creature fully itself. And at the end of the sixth day, looking at all of it together: "and, behold, it was very good." Six days of making, and the chapter keeps count of the good.
screen: `THREE DAYS OF ROOMS.` · `THREE DAYS TO FILL THEM.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · `EACH AFTER ITS KIND.` · then, large: `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Open your eyes and look around, slowly, and name six good things you can see, one for each day. Something with light in it. Something from the sky, even just the air or a window. Something that grew. Something that shines. Something alive. And a person, or a trace of one: a photo, a handwritten note, your own hands. Say each one quietly, then let the list sit. The bell holds the time.
Six days of making. Three days of rooms, three days of filling them, and the good counted all the way through.
Your line: count the good. Tonight, before bed, count six good things from today, out loud or on your fingers, one for each day of making. Day twenty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read the six days of creation in the first Torah portion each autumn, and in the daily morning prayers praise God who renews the work of creation every day.

original.note: Hebrew: day. each day of making closes with evening and morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of what God made when.
what it means: a chapter built like a house: three days of rooms, three of filling them, and the good counted throughout.
what a scholar hears: the forming-and-filling pattern; Chagigah 12a says the first light was hidden for the righteous; Genesis 1:16 never names the sun and moon, only the greater and lesser lights.
